_comment: The Maize Genetics Executive Committee record behind /mgec.
Transcribed on 2026-09-05 from the twenty templates this page replaced:
templates/community/mgec-content.bau      mission statement, document archive
templates/community/mgec-origins.bau      the 1929-2000 timeline
templates/community/mgec-procedures.bau   March 2004 procedures, 2018/2019 motions
templates/community/mgec-committees.bau   21 terms of rosters
templates/community/mgec-activities<year>.bau   16 activity reports, 2000-2019
Those files are archived in legacy/mgec/ and their routes now redirect here.
The roster transcription was checked against the source: 42 distinct names on
both sides. The source lists 194 member lines to this file's 193 because the
2007-08 roster names Sarah Hake twice, once as chair and once as a member.
Three terms -- 2006-07, 2005-06 and 2002-03 -- are recorded in the source with
no roster, and are kept here with an empty member list so the gap stays
visible rather than looking like an omission.
`dead: true` marks a link whose target no longer resolves, checked 2026-09-05.
Those entries keep their label and lose their link, so the record still says
the document existed. Six are dead: maizeresearch.org (domain gone), three
ncga.com PDFs (404), and the 2016 and 2017 community survey reports, which
return HTTP 500 from community.maizegdb.org. Everything else was verified to
return a real body, not just a 200.
Meeting minutes are a record and are kept verbatim, including their typos.

origins.text: First Maize Genetics Meeting, at Allerton House in Illinois
Plan for a Vision/History Meeting at Allerton
Ed Coe forms an ad hoc vision committee
Allerton discussion on the future of maize genetics
Survey of the maize genetics community by the ad hoc vision committee
Ed Coe organizes a future-of-maize discussion at the Plant and Animal Genome 2000 conference
Ad hoc committee develops a plan for a Maize Genetics Executive Committee elected by the entire maize genetics community

First Maize Genetics Executive Committee elected: Jeff Bennetzen (chair), Jim Birchler, Vicki Chandler, Ed Coe, Mike Freeling, Sarah Hake, Ron Phillips, Pat Schnable, Virginia Walbot and Sue Wessler. Jane Langdale was asked to join the MGEC to provide international perspective
Maize Genetics Executive Committee conceives its mission statement, develops guidelines for its operations, and begins communicating with the genetics community and the broader scientific community

items: Ad hoc committee organizes and runs the election for the MGEC. Over 300 votes received and ten members elected: Jeff Bennetzen, Jim Birchler, Ed Coe, Vicki Chandler, Mike Freeling, Sarah Hake, Ron Phillips, Pat Schnable, Ginny Walbot and Sue Wessler.
Committee elects an MGEC chair (Bennetzen), a vice-chair (Coe) and an overseas member (Jane Langdale).

Committee discusses a possible mission for the MGEC and decides on a role of acquiring, collating, interpreting and disseminating information on the opportunities and needs for maize genetics research in the public sector.
Committee solicits and begins collation of information from the maize genetics community on needed technical advances for maize genetics.

A subcommittee travels to Washington, DC and meets with NSF geneticists and plant scientists to discuss the identified highest-priority need, improved maize transformation technology. USDA participants were unable to attend because of a last-minute facilities problem but received a report of the discussion. Both NSF and USDA subsequently featured a need for improved maize transformation technology in their RFPs.

MGEC discusses several issues related to improving the visibility and productivity of maize genetics research in the public sector. Three documents — Highest Priorities, A 10-Year Plan, and a draft letter to members of Congress — were promulgated.
MGEC assists MaizeDB in its efforts to review its performance, and encourages a simplified entry route to all maize databases.
A workshop on sequencing the maize genome was conducted in 2001. An executive summary and report were prepared and promulgated.

Continued solicitation and encouragement of U.S. governmental commitment to sequence the maize genome, with visits to Washington, DC and the preparation and distribution of a white paper. The outcome was an RFP from NSF requesting proposals to test technologies for the efficient sequencing of complex plant genomes; two proposals were funded, to test gene-rich BAC and gene-enrichment sequencing approaches in maize.
First web presence for the MGEC, acquired through MaizeDB.
Discussion of an annual maize genetics course that could recruit and train young scientists for maize genetics. Candidate sites were identified.

Discussions with Congressional staffers and USAID personnel, including visits to Washington, DC, to encourage a competitive grants program through USAID supporting comparative cereal genomics for agricultural improvement in the developing world. The outcome was a small grants program, managed by Dr. Robert Zeigler at Kansas State University, initiated in 2002.
Nominations and election to available MGEC seats.

Solicitation and collation of suggestions from the maize genetics community for a new poll asking all maize geneticists about the prioritized needs of the community. The poll was planned for mid-2003.

Organized a workshop, as part of the 2003 Maize Genetics Conference, to discuss alternative technologies for the global profiling of maize transcripts. Met with representatives from commercial vendors, considered the platforms, and submitted recommendations to the National Science Foundation.

Developed and submitted to the National Science Foundation a work plan for sequencing the maize genome. V. Chandler presented the work plan to the Inter-agency Working Group in Washington, DC on February 22, at a meeting with industry representatives.

Worked with the National Corn Growers Association, DuPont-Pioneer, Monsanto and Ceres to reach an agreement by which more than two million maize ESTs previously generated by the private sector could be accessed by public-sector researchers.

Formalized election dates and terms of office for MGEC members, established election procedures, rotation and selection of the chair, and defined a practice for selecting additional representative members, adding two members on that basis. The procedures are in the Procedures section of this page.
Encouraged development of a short course in maize genetics held at CIMMYT alongside the 2004 Maize Genetics Conference.
Worked with the National Corn Growers Association to help them communicate the importance of maize genome sequence to scientists and farmers.
Contributed to the Cereal Genomics course at Cold Spring Harbor in September 2005. The initial idea for the course came from the MGEC.
Organized and edited a maize genomics section for Current Opinion in Plant Biology, to which three members of the MGEC contributed.
Worked with the National Corn Growers Association to help them communicate the importance of maize genome sequence to scientists and farmers.
Developed a survey that went to all maize genetics community members, synthesized it, and posted the results on MaizeGDB. The results were also sent to funding agencies and to the NCGA.
Committee members Ed Buckler and Jo Messing spoke at the Post Maize Genome Sequence meeting for the NCGA in August 2006.
Initiated plans for a new comprehensive Maize Handbook, edited by Jeff Bennetzen and Sarah Hake.
April 2010. MGEC chair Tom Brutnell presented an overview of the 2009 MGEC survey at a National Corn Growers Association workshop. Pat Schnable and Steve Moose also gave presentations.
May 2010. Deployment of the Maize Research Blog.
September 8, 2010. The MGEC met with NSF to discuss the concerns of, and opportunities for, the maize genetics community.

December 2010. As a direct result of the meeting with NSF, established the Maize Genome Assembly and Annotation Consortium, first announced in the maize workshop at the 2011 Plant and Animal Genome conference. NSF funds were requested from the Plant Genome Research Program in a January 2011 submission.

docs.label: MGEC report on the September 2010 NSF meeting

items: March 18, 2011. The committee met with representatives of USDA-ARS, NSF and the National Corn Growers Association. The full minutes are below.

minutes.title: Maize Genetics Executive Committee meeting, March 18, 2011
minutes.attendance: Tom Brutnell (chair), Pat Schnable, Bill Tracy, Sue Wessler, Ed Buckler, Carolyn Lawrence, Brent Buckner, and two new members, Nathan Springer and Marja Timmermans. Guests: Jack Okamuro from USDA-ARS, Rick Vierling from NCGA, and Karen Cone from NSF.

sections.heading: NCGA (Vierling)
paragraphs: There was much discussion about growers' potential dissatisfaction with apparent lack of translation of discovery science to application. Clearly, a large part of this is communication. The maize community should think of ways of being more proactive with the growers - perhaps a Maize Genetics Blog on the NCGA web site or a link to a blog at MaizeGDB to inform of how major breakthoughs are having impact. A set of one pagers of newsworthy maize stories was suggested as one mechanism that could be used to emphasize important discoveries for the popular press, members of Congress of web posts. There was also discussion of performing growouts of NAM populations in farmers' fields as test plots for phenotyping. Vierling mentioned a potential to partner with NCGA for yield trials and that the USFRA (US Farmers and Ranchers Alliance) could be involved. This would be one way to engage farmers directly with basic science.

sections.heading: USDA (Okamuro)
paragraphs: Many ARS scientists are in National Program 301 (Plant genetic resources, genomics, and genetic improvement), which is in its 5th year cycle and about to start a customer/stakeholder workshop. Input is desired for the current needs, issues, and challenges in the field. University partners and stakeholders are welcome to contribute. For maize, ARS supports genetics, genomics, databases, and computational tool development. Thus far for FY2011, a ~$140M cut has been absorbed. The stock center is not affected thus far. For maintenance of B73 genome, there was an update at PAG and there was another update at the maize meeting. The MaizeGDB Working Group reports on this topic were received by the ARS National Program Staff and NPS will also be willing to take guidance from the MGEC on B73 genome stewardship.

sections.heading: NSF (Cone)
paragraphs: Cone emphasized that what NSF wants to fund is compatible with the maize genetics research community and there are new funding opportunities. For example, G2P is a new collaboration with USDA NIFA to have new direction in phenomics and there will be a St. Louis workshop on phenomics coming soon. Rob Last and Tim Close are serving to organize this event. There is an emphasis on international collaboration including a solicitation on metabolomics with Japan's equivalent of the Office of International Science and Engineering (OISE) to serve as a “new collaborator incubator”. The NSF OISE's new administrative director is Machi Dilworth. BREAD also emphasizes international collaboration.

sections.heading: Need to store large datasets
paragraphs: Other topics discussed with NSF, USDA, and the Corn Growers.

NCBI SRA is closing except to human datasets (this policy has subsequently been reversed, but it is not clear how long SRA will be open to plant scientists). Buckler, Lawrence, and iPlant are open to making changes for large dat
There was concern that PGRP will lose its impact in IOS. In 2012 there was no line item. Vierling mentioned that NCGA and growers want to see PGRP continued.

sections.heading: Discussion on the 2010 meeting with NSF
paragraphs: Buckler, Brutnell, Walbot, Lawrence met with Diane Okamuro and Jane Silverthorne. Main points were (1) that we need new genome assembly and build mechanisms and that the data should be hosted and stored, (2) community annotation is needed, (3) basic, single-investigator granting opportunities are not apparent, and (4) help for funding the Maize Genetics Cooperation - Stock Center are needed.

sections.heading: Sequencing projects at BGI in China
paragraphs: There is growing sequence capacity at BGI in China and many in the community are beginning to use this resource. However, sequence access and visualization do not seem to be priorities of BGI. Although data should be provided to GenBank prior to publication, it is not clear that publishers are enforcing this rule. Reviewers should be more insistent on this point. US collaborators with BGI need to get a copy of the sequence and RELEASE IT. Authors should communicate to editors, talk to reviewers, and alert the community that this is an issue. It was noted that this should not be an issue because people want to publish their papers and the publishers have the ability to enforce this rule. They just need to be more diligent.

sections.heading: Plant Summit planned for end of September by ASPB
paragraphs: It was noted that a Plant Science Research Summit is planned to bring attention to plant science and begin a dialog aimed at increasing funding for plant science research. Members of the MGEC in attendance at the Plant Science Summit included Bennetzen, Brutnell, Buckler, Buckner, Lawrence and Schnable.

sections.heading: Stock Center
paragraphs: The Stock Center experienced the untimely death of Janet Day Jackson. Marty is currently putting in the paperwork to allow him to refill the position but, at the time of this report (Nov 2011), has been unable to do so.

minutes.signoff: — Tom Brutnell on behalf of the MGEC, November 2011.
